lessons.title: The Fracture Points: 2008, the US-China Trade War, COVID and the Russia-Ukraine Shock

children.text: In March 2020, Indian pharmaceutical companies discovered how much of their supply chain they did not actually control. China's Hubei lockdown had cut factory output right at the source of the raw material Indian drugmakers depend on most: active pharmaceutical ingredients, or APIs, the chemical compounds that go into every tablet. For a country that calls itself the pharmacy of the world, having roughly two-thirds of its API needs sourced from a single foreign country was not a fact anyone had needed to think about, until suddenly it was the only fact that mattered. The previous lesson traced how the postwar trading system was built. This lesson traces how four shocks, in just fourteen years, exposed what that system had quietly stopped accounting for: resilience.

body.text: Hyperglobalization was not undone by any single event. It was undone by four shocks in fourteen years, each one breaking a different assumption the postwar trading system had been quietly built on.

children.text: 2008: The First Break in Trade Growth

From China's WTO accession in 2001 through 2008, world trade had grown consistently faster than world GDP, the defining feature of hyperglobalization. The Global Financial Crisis broke that pattern in a single year. World merchandise trade volumes fell by roughly 12% in 2009, the sharpest contraction since the Second World War, as global credit froze and demand for everything from container shipping to trade finance collapsed overnight.

Trade rebounded sharply in 2010, but the trend line never fully returned to its pre-2008 slope. Trade as a share of world GDP, which had climbed almost without interruption since 1960, peaked around 2008 and then flattened for the next decade. Commentators later gave this plateau a name:

, trade still growing, but no longer outrunning the world economy the way it had for the previous three decades. India, with a banking system relatively insulated from the US subprime crisis, avoided the worst of the direct financial contagion, but still saw sharp FII outflows and a Sensex fall of more than 50% from its January 2008 peak to its trough, a reminder that Indian equities were now wired into the same global cycle as everyone else.

The second break was not economic, it was political. Washington opened a Section 301 investigation into China's technology transfer practices in August 2017, and by July 2018 had begun imposing tariffs directly. Beijing retaliated in kind. Over the next eighteen months, both sides escalated repeatedly.

cells: US opens a Section 301 investigation into China's IP and technology transfer practices
US imposes 25% tariffs on the first tranche of Chinese imports; China retaliates the same day
Multiple further tranches; by September 2019 US tariffs cover roughly $370 billion of Chinese imports, Chinese retaliatory tariffs cover roughly $110 billion of US imports
Phase One deal signed; tariff escalation pauses, most existing tariffs remain in place

body.text: India was not a direct party to the US-China trade war, but it was not a bystander either. As multinational buyers looked to diversify sourcing away from China, India picked up incremental export share in categories like furniture, textiles and low-end electronics assembly, an early, small-scale preview of the China+1 shift this course returns to in Chapter 3.

body.title: Size the trade war
body.prompt: By September 2019, US tariffs covered roughly $370 billion of Chinese imports and Chinese retaliatory tariffs covered roughly $110 billion of US imports. Approximately how much two-way trade, in USD billion, had tariffs been applied to in total?
body.explanation: $370 billion plus $110 billion is approximately $480 billion of two-way trade caught up in tariffs, out of roughly $650 billion in total US-China goods trade at the time. That is the majority of the entire bilateral trading relationship.

children.text: 2020-2021: COVID-19 and the Supply Chain Shock

COVID-19 did not just disrupt trade, it revealed how little slack the hyperglobalized system carried. Decades of just-in-time manufacturing, built to minimise inventory and cost, meant that a single-source disruption anywhere could halt production everywhere. Container shipping rates were the clearest market signal of the strain: spot rates on the Shanghai to Los Angeles route rose from roughly $1,500 to $2,000 per 40-foot container in 2019 to more than $20,000 at the 2021 peak.

body.label: Shanghai-Los Angeles container freight rate, 2019 vs 2021 peak
body.context: A more than tenfold increase in the cost of moving a single 40-foot container, a direct tax on every globally sourced product.

body.title: India's Bulk Drug (API) Import Sources, FY21

children.text: That concentration is exactly what shut down Indian pharma production lines in early 2020, and it is why the government later launched a Production Linked Incentive scheme specifically for bulk drugs and key starting materials, a policy response this course examines in more depth in Chapter 4. The semiconductor shortage that followed, as chip fabs ran below capacity while demand for laptops and cars whipsawed, showed the same lesson playing out globally: efficiency and resilience are not the same goal, and the system had been optimised almost entirely for the former.
2022: Russia's Invasion of Ukraine and the Weaponization of Trade

markDefs.definition: Using access to a country's financial infrastructure, such as the SWIFT messaging network or a central bank's foreign reserves, as an instrument of foreign policy rather than a neutral utility.

children.text: The fourth shock broke an assumption the previous three had left standing: that deep economic interdependence made large-scale interstate conflict too costly to happen, and that global financial infrastructure was neutral, available to any country regardless of politics. Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 was met with the exclusion of major Russian banks from SWIFT and the freezing of a large share of Russia's foreign exchange reserves held abroad, an early and stark example of

. Energy markets fractured next, as Europe raced to cut its dependence on Russian gas, and food and fertiliser prices spiked globally, since Russia and Ukraine together were major exporters of wheat, sunflower oil and fertiliser inputs.

India's response is a case study in pragmatic non-alignment that this course returns to repeatedly. Russia supplied under 2% of India's crude oil imports before the invasion. Within about a year, discounted Urals crude had made Russia India's single largest source of crude oil, well over a third of total imports, refined in large volumes by Reliance Industries and state-owned refiners and, in significant part, re-exported as diesel and other refined products to Europe and elsewhere, a trade India navigated using rupee and non-dollar settlement mechanisms with Russian counterparties.

body.title: Assess the crude oil pivot
body.scenario: An Indian public-sector refiner is deciding how much of its crude oil procurement to shift toward discounted Russian Urals crude, given the price discount versus traditional Gulf suppliers, but also given the risk of secondary sanctions exposure, shipping and insurance complications, and the diplomatic sensitivity of the relationship with Western partners.
body.prompt: As a macro analyst, list the three factors you would weigh most heavily in projecting whether this shift in crude sourcing is likely to persist over the next two to three years, or unwind.
body.modelAnswer: Reasonable factors include: (1) the size of the price discount on Urals crude versus Gulf benchmarks, and whether it remains wide enough to offset the added logistics and insurance costs, (2) the trajectory of Western sanctions enforcement, particularly the G7 price cap mechanism and any tightening of secondary sanctions on shippers, insurers or refiners, and (3) India's own strategic calculus around energy security and diversification, since import dependence on any single supplier, discounted or not, recreates the same concentration risk this lesson has already shown can turn into a shock. A strong answer should note that India has historically preferred to keep multiple large suppliers active precisely to avoid over-concentration, even while taking advantage of temporary discounts.

cells: That trade would keep growing faster than GDP indefinitely
That MFN tariff discipline was politically untouchable between major powers
That optimising supply chains purely for efficiency was more valuable than building in resilience
That economic interdependence prevents open conflict, and that financial infrastructure is politically neutral

body.title: Name the term
body.textWithBlank: The plateau in world trade's share of GDP after its 2008 peak, in which trade kept growing but no longer consistently outpaced the global economy, is commonly called ___.
body.explanation: Slowbalisation describes the post-2008 pattern precisely: trade did not collapse or reverse, it simply stopped accelerating faster than GDP, the defining feature of the hyperglobalization era covered in the previous lesson.

cards.definition: The post-2008 plateau in world trade as a share of GDP, trade still growing but no longer consistently outpacing the global economy.
The US trade law provision used to investigate and impose tariffs on China starting in 2017-2018, the legal basis for the US-China trade war.
A production strategy that minimises inventory by timing input deliveries closely to need, efficient in normal conditions but fragile to single-source disruption, as COVID-19 exposed.
Using access to systems like SWIFT or foreign exchange reserves as a tool of foreign policy, illustrated starkly by the sanctions imposed on Russia from 2022.

points: Four shocks in fourteen years, 2008, 2018-2019, 2020-2021 and 2022, each broke a different assumption the postwar trading system had been built on.
The 2008 financial crisis ended the pattern of trade consistently outgrowing global GDP, giving way to a slower-growth pattern later termed slowbalisation.
The 2018-2019 US-China trade war applied tariffs to roughly $480 billion of two-way trade, showing MFN discipline between major powers was no longer politically untouchable.
COVID-19 exposed how single-source dependencies, like India's roughly two-thirds reliance on China for API imports, turn an efficiency strategy into a resilience risk.

The 2022 Russia-Ukraine war showed that financial infrastructure itself, not just goods and tariffs, can be weaponized, reshaping how countries including India think about counterparty and currency risk in trade.

India's response across these shocks, from FDI liberalization type openness to opportunistic, non-aligned sourcing of discounted Russian crude, is a recurring case study in how a large emerging economy navigates a fragmenting order.
